case_info.explanation: C. Prescribe 40-mg prednisone daily for 14 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the presence of a linear depression along a superficial vein, visible when the forearm is raised, which is characteristic of eosinophilic fasciitis. Topical clobetasol (choice A) is incorrect because eosinophilic fasciitis consists of deeper fascial sclerosis that is not adequately treated by topical steroids.1,2High-dose immunoglobulin (choice B) and mycophenolate mofetil (choice D) are not first-line treatments for eosinophilic fasciitis.3 Eosinophilic fasciitis is rare, with fewer than 600 reported cases worldwide, has no known etiology, and typically affects adults aged 30 to 60 years.4Patients initially develop subacute pain, erythema, and nonpitting edema of limbs or trunk that progresses to symmetric deep, woody skin induration over months to years.4Collagenous thickening of the subcutaneous fascia gives the skin an “orange peel” appearance.4Fibrosis and tethering of connective tissue around superficial veins cause the venous groove sign—a linear depression resulting from overlying epidermis being pulled inward along a vein.4 Eosinophilic fasciitis is associated with hematologic malignancies (eg, Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, multiple myeloma), graft-vs-host disease, hemodialysis initiation, radiation therapy, and  sustained intense physical exertion such as running. Based on case reports and small case series, certain medications are associated with eosinophilic fasciitis, including immune checkpoint inhibitors (eg, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab), statins, and proton pump inhibitors (eg, esomeprazole, lansoprazole).3,5 The criterion standard for the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis is presence of dermal and fascial fibrosis with or without eosinophils on a wedge biopsy that includes skin, subcutaneous fat, and fascia.1However, in some cases the diagnosis may be made clinically in patients who have nonpitting edema or symmetric induration in distal limbs; MRI findings of fascial thickening with hyperintense T2 signal and contrast enhancement; and supportive but nonspecific laboratory findings, such as elevated inflammatory markers (eg, C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and hypergammaglobulinemia.4,6Prior to treatment with steroids, most patients initially have peripheral eosinophilia.3,7 The differential diagnosis includes systemic sclerosis, scleromyxedema and scleredema, and eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (associated with consumption of L-tryptophan or 5-hydroxytryptophan supplements).4,8Patients with eosinophilic fasciitis have cutaneous fibrosis but lack other characteristic features of systemic sclerosis, including digital and facial skin sclerosis, nailfold capillary abnormalities, Raynaud phenomenon, visceral involvement (eg, esophageal dysfunction, interstitial lung disease, scleroderma renal crisis), and specific autoantibodies such as antitopoisomerase I (Scl-70), anticentromere, anti-RNA polymerase III, and anti-U3-RNP (fibrillarin).4Differentiating eosinophilic fasciitis from systemic sclerosis is important because in patients with systemic sclerosis, steroids can trigger renal crisis, which involves a sudden-onset, severe increase in blood pressure and rapid decline in kidney function.9 First-line treatment for eosinophilic fasciitis is oral prednisone (0.5-1 mg/kg daily), although 3 days of intravenous methylprednisolone (500-1000 mg) may be used in severe cases.7Steroid doses are tapered based on clinical response, and more than 70% of patients have complete resolution of cutaneous swelling after taking prednisone for several months, although the groove sign may persist several years after treatment.2,4Immunosuppressants such as methotrexate and mycophenolate mofetil may be added for extensive disease or to help taper or discontinue steroids.4,9,10Based on case series, tocilizumab, baricitinib, infliximab, rituximab, or intravenous immunoglobulins may be effective for severe eosinophilic fasciitis.3Physical therapy to prevent limb contractures is recommended for all patients with eosinophilic fasciitis.3 Eosinophilic fasciitis was diagnosed based on the patient’s history, venous groove sign, and characteristic findings on MRI. After 1 month of treatment with oral prednisone (40 mg daily), she gained 4.54 kg (10 lb), so oral methotrexate (20 mg weekly) with folic acid (1 mg daily) was initiated, and the prednisone dose was tapered over 3 months. She underwent physical therapy twice weekly and was advised to take oral calcium (1000 mg daily) and vitamin D (1000 IU daily) due to concerns about adverse effects on bone associated with steroid use and to use contraception due to potential teratogenicity of methotrexate. At most recent follow-up 6 months after initial presentation, the skin tightening on her bilateral forearms and shins had decreased and her hand and elbow mobility had improved, but the groove sign on the right forearm persisted.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },

  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Prescribe 40-mg prednisone daily for 14 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the presence of a linear depression along a superficial vein, visible when the forearm is raised, which is characteristic of eosinophilic fasciitis. Topical clobetasol (choice A) is incorrect because eosinophilic fasciitis consists of deeper fascial sclerosis that is not adequately treated by topical steroids.1,2High-dose immunoglobulin (choice B) and mycophenolate mofetil (choice D) are not first-line treatments for eosinophilic fasciitis.3 Eosinophilic fasciitis is rare, with fewer than 600 reported cases worldwide, has no known etiology, and typically affects adults aged 30 to 60 years.4Patients initially develop subacute pain, erythema, and nonpitting edema of limbs or trunk that progresses to symmetric deep, woody skin induration over months to years.4Collagenous thickening of the subcutaneous fascia gives the skin an “orange peel” appearance.4Fibrosis and tethering of connective tissue around superficial veins cause the venous groove sign—a linear depression resulting from overlying epidermis being pulled inward along a vein.4 Eosinophilic fasciitis is associated with hematologic malignancies (eg, Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, multiple myeloma), graft-vs-host disease, hemodialysis initiation, radiation therapy, and  sustained intense physical exertion such as running. Based on case reports and small case series, certain medications are associated with eosinophilic fasciitis, including immune checkpoint inhibitors (eg, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab), statins, and proton pump inhibitors (eg, esomeprazole, lansoprazole).3,5 The criterion standard for the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis is presence of dermal and fascial fibrosis with or without eosinophils on a wedge biopsy that includes skin, subcutaneous fat, and fascia.1However, in some cases the diagnosis may be made clinically in patients who have nonpitting edema or symmetric induration in distal You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Topical clobetasol (choice A) is incorrect because eosinophilic fasciitis consists of deeper fascial sclerosis that is not adequately treated by topical steroids.1,2High-dose immunoglobulin (choice B) and mycophenolate mofetil (choice D) are not first-line treatments for eosinophilic fasciitis.3 Eosinophilic fasciitis is rare, with fewer than 600 reported cases worldwide, has no known etiology, and typically affects adults aged 30 to 60 years.4Patients initially develop subacute pain, erythema, and nonpitting edema of limbs or trunk that progresses to symmetric deep, woody skin induration over months to years.4Collagenous thickening of the subcutaneous fascia gives the skin an “orange peel” appearance.4Fibrosis and tethering of connective tissue around superficial veins cause the venous groove sign—a linear depression resulting from overlying epidermis being pulled inward along a vein.4 Eosinophilic fasciitis is associated with hematologic malignancies (eg, Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, multiple myeloma), graft-vs-host disease, hemodialysis initiation, radiation therapy, and  sustained intense physical exertion such as running. Based on case reports and small case series, certain medications are associated with eosinophilic fasciitis, including immune checkpoint inhibitors (eg, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab), statins, and proton pump inhibitors (eg, esomeprazole, lansoprazole).3,5 The criterion standard for the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis is presence of dermal and fascial fibrosis with or without eosinophils on a wedge biopsy that includes skin, subcutaneous fat, and fascia.1However, in some cases the diagnosis may be made clinically in patients who have nonpitting edema or symmetric induration in distal limbs; MRI findings of fascial thickening with hyperintense T2 signal and contrast enhancement; and supportive but nonspecific laboratory findings, such as elevated inflammatory markers (eg, C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and hypergammaglobulinemia.4,6Prior to treatment with steroids, most patients initially have peripheral eosinophilia.3,7 The differential diagnosis includes systemic sclerosis, scleromyxedema and scleredema, and eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (associated with consumption of L-tryptophan or 5-hydroxytryptophan supplements).4,8Patients with eosinophilic fasciitis have cutaneous fibrosis but lack other characteristic features of systemic sclerosis, including digital and facial skin sclerosis, nailfold capillary abnormalities, Raynaud phenomenon, visceral involvement (eg, esophageal dysfunction, interstitial lung disease, scleroderma renal crisis), and specific autoantibodies such as antitopoisomerase I (Scl-70), anticentromere, anti-RNA polymerase III, and anti-U3-RNP (fibrillarin).4Differentiating eosinophilic fasciitis from systemic sclerosis is important because in patients with systemic sclerosis, steroids can trigger renal crisis, which involves a sudden-onset, severe increase in blood pressure and rapid decline in kidney function.9 First-line treatment for eosinophilic fasciitis is oral prednisone (0.5-1 mg/kg daily), although 3 days of intravenous methylprednisolone (500-1000 mg) may be used in severe cases.7Steroid doses are tapered based on clinical response, and more than 70% of patients have complete resolution of cutaneous swelling after taking prednisone for several months, although the groove sign may persist several years after treatment.2,4Immunosuppressants such as methotrexate and mycophenolate mofetil may be added for extensive disease or to help taper or discontinue steroids.4,9,10Based on case series, tocilizumab, baricitinib, infliximab, rituximab, or intravenous immunoglobulins may be effective for severe eosinophilic fasciitis.3Physical therapy to prevent limb contractures is recommended for all patients with eosinophilic fasciitis.3 Eosinophilic fasciitis deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact

- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;

Prescribe 40-mg prednisone daily for 14 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the presence of a linear depression along a superficial vein, visible when the forearm is raised, which is characteristic of eosinophilic fasciitis. Topical clobetasol (choice A) is incorrect because eosinophilic fasciitis consists of deeper fascial sclerosis that is not adequately treated by topical steroids.1,2High-dose immunoglobulin (choice B) and mycophenolate mofetil (choice D) are not first-line treatments for eosinophilic fasciitis.3 Eosinophilic fasciitis is rare, with fewer than 600 reported cases worldwide, has no known etiology, and typically affects adults aged 30 to 60 years.4Patients initially develop subacute pain, erythema, and nonpitting edema of limbs or trunk that progresses to symmetric deep, woody skin induration over months to years.4Collagenous thickening of the subcutaneous fascia gives the skin an “orange peel” appearance.4Fibrosis and tethering of connective tissue around superficial veins cause the venous groove sign—a linear depression resulting from overlying epidermis being pulled inward along a vein.4 Eosinophilic fasciitis is associated with hematologic malignancies (eg, Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, multiple myeloma), graft-vs-host disease, hemodialysis initiation, radiation therapy, and  sustained intense physical exertion such as running. Based on case reports and small case series, certain medications are associated with eosinophilic fasciitis, including immune checkpoint inhibitors (eg, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab), statins, and proton pump inhibitors (eg, esomeprazole, lansoprazole).3,5 The criterion standard for the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis is presence of dermal and fascial fibrosis with or without eosinophils on a wedge biopsy that includes skin, subcutaneous fat, and fascia.1However, in some cases the diagnosis may be made clinically in patients who have nonpitting edema or symmetric induration in distal limbs; MRI findings of fascial thickening with hyperintense T2 signal and contrast enhancement; and supportive but nonspecific laboratory findings, such as elevated inflammatory markers (eg, C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and hypergammaglobulinemia.4,6Prior to treatment with steroids, most patients initially have peripheral eosinophilia.3,7 The differential diagnosis includes systemic sclerosis, scleromyxedema and scleredema, and eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (associated with consumption of L-tryptophan or 5-hydroxytryptophan supplements).4,8Patients with eosinophilic fasciitis have cutaneous fibrosis but lack other characteristic features of systemic sclerosis, including digital and facial skin sclerosis, nailfold capillary abnormalities, Raynaud phenomenon, visceral involvement (eg, esophageal dysfunction, interstitial lung disease, scleroderma renal crisis), and specific autoantibodies such as antitopoisomerase I (Scl-70), anticentromere, anti-RNA polymerase III, and anti-U3-RNP (fibrillarin).4Differentiating eosinophilic fasciitis from systemic sclerosis is important because in patients with systemic sclerosis, steroids can trigger renal crisis, which involves a sudden-onset, severe increase in blood pressure and rapid decline in kidney function.9 First-line treatment for eosinophilic fasciitis is oral prednisone (0.5-1 mg/kg daily), although 3 days of intravenous methylprednisolone (500-1000 mg) may be used in severe cases.7Steroid doses are tapered based on clinical response, and more than 70% of patients have complete resolution of cutaneous swelling after taking prednisone for several months, although the groove sign may persist several years after treatment.2,4Immunosuppressants such as methotrexate and mycophenolate mofetil may be added for extensive disease or to help taper or discontinue steroids.4,9,10Based on case series, tocilizumab, baricitinib, infliximab, rituximab, or intravenous immunoglobulins may be effective for severe eosinophilic fasciitis.3Physical therapy to prevent limb contractures is recommended for all patients with eosinophilic fasciitis.3 Eosinophilic fasciitis was diagnosed based on the patient’s history, venous groove sign, and characteristic findings on MRI. After 1 month of treatment with oral prednisone (40 mg daily), she gained 4.54 kg (10 lb), so oral methotrexate (20 mg weekly) with folic acid (1 mg daily) was initiated, and the prednisone dose was tapered over 3 months. ## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a

               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.
